blocks.text: Before the oil boom, cocoa, palm oil, groundnuts and cotton paid for Nigeria's imports. After it, crude oil came to dominate export receipts and the Federation Account, while many farms and factories lost workers to the cities. Understanding that shift — agriculture's enduring role, petroleum's mixed blessing, and the strategies used to industrialise — is the last piece of the secondary Economics syllabus.

blocks.markdown:
**Agriculture** still employs a large share of the labour force and supplies food, industrial raw materials (cotton, rubber, cassava, oil palm) and some non-oil foreign exchange (cocoa, sesame). Most production remains **peasant and smallholder**, with mixed cropping, limited irrigation and simple tools.

Problems are structural rather than a single bad harvest: **communal and fragmented land tenure** that discourages long-term investment; **poor storage** and rural roads, so tomatoes rot between farm and market; inadequate rural credit; pests, drought and flooding; ageing farmers as the young migrate; and years in which cheap food imports and an oil-backed naira undercut local output.

blocks.title: Dutch disease
blocks.text: A pattern in which a boom in one export — in Nigeria, crude oil — draws labour and capital away from other tradable sectors, and a stronger currency (or neglect of those sectors) makes farms and factories less competitive. Agriculture and manufacturing shrink as a share of exports even if they remain large in employment. The name comes from the Netherlands' gas boom; the mechanism is what examiners want.

blocks.markdown:
### Petroleum in the Nigerian economy

Commercial oil production from the late 1950s, and the price shocks of the 1970s, turned crude into the fiscal and foreign-exchange backbone of the state. The **Nigerian National Petroleum Company** (now operating as NNPCL) is the national oil company, partnering with international firms, holding equity in joint ventures and running (or overseeing) refineries and the downstream system.

Oil pays for much of what FAAC shares, so a fall in the dollar price of crude immediately squeezes federal, state and local budgets and the naira's supply of foreign exchange. The industry is an **enclave**: high in value, modest in direct employment, geographically concentrated in the Niger Delta, and historically better linked to tanker terminals than to local manufacturing. Environmental damage and theft are part of the same story. A durable lesson of the syllabus is **diversification**: grow non-oil taxes, revive agriculture and build industry so that one commodity cannot dictate the exchange rate and the budget together.

items: **Import substitution industrialisation (ISI)** — produce locally what used to be imported, behind tariffs and licences. Nigeria used this from the 1960s into the early 1980s (textiles, assembly, brewing). It saved some foreign exchange but often produced high-cost goods and a hunger for imported inputs and machinery.
**Export promotion** — make manufactures and processed crops competitive abroad, with realistic exchange rates, less protection, and attention to quality. This was a stated aim after reform.

**Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP), 1986** — naira devaluation, fewer import licences, privatisation, interest-rate and trade liberalisation, aimed at restoring price signals and a viable BOP. Effects were mixed: some export crops recovered, but real wages and manufacturing capacity were hit, and the social cost was high.

**Later reforms** — banking consolidation, a more active NGX, power-sector unbundling, agricultural programmes, and large private industrial projects (including domestic refining) that try to keep more of the oil value chain at home.

blocks.title: Evaluating a policy mix for diversification
blocks.prompt: A minister argues: 'Because oil still dominates exports, we should raise tariffs on all imports, freeze the naira at a strong rate, and expand peasant farming with more fertilizer only.' Using comparative advantage, Dutch disease and SAP-era lessons, evaluate this package.

steps.text: A strong, possibly overvalued naira is part of Dutch disease: it cheapens imports and punishes non-oil exports, so it works against both agriculture and manufacturing.
Blanket tariffs repeat the ISI error — they protect inefficiency and raise costs for factories that need imported spare parts, without creating comparative advantage.
Fertilizer for peasant farms can raise food output, but without storage, tenure reform, rural roads and credit the extra harvest may still not reach the market.

A more coherent mix would be: a competitive (not artificially strong) naira, targeted support for storage and land rights, export promotion in agro-processing, and tariffs only where an infant industry has a clear learning path.
SAP showed that price correction alone is not enough, but it also showed that suppressing prices and rationing foreign exchange does not rebuild farms and factories.

blocks.answer: The package fights the symptoms with tools that worsen Dutch disease; diversification needs a competitive naira, targeted farm-to-market investment and selective — not blanket — protection

blocks.title: Give roles and problems, then a balanced judgement
blocks.text: WAEC theory questions on the Nigerian economy are won by structure: two roles of agriculture, three problems, one oil-related concept (Dutch disease or revenue volatility), and a brief evaluation of ISI versus export promotion or SAP. Do not invent a current official oil-price or GDP-growth figure as if it were a syllabus fact — describe mechanisms instead.

points: Agriculture provides food, jobs, raw materials and some exports, but is held back by peasant scale, land tenure, storage, finance and migration.
Petroleum dominates export earnings and federally collected revenue; NNPC/NNPCL is the national oil company; volatility, theft, weak refining and Dutch disease are the core problems.
ISI built factories behind protection; export promotion seeks competitiveness abroad.
SAP (1986) liberalised trade and the naira with mixed social and industrial results.
Diversification — non-oil revenue, agro-industry, domestic refining and a competitive exchange rate — is the recurring policy conclusion.
